metaDescription: Gas snow blowers compared on engine, drive system, intake size and upkeep, from tracked 28-inch machines to compact single-stage units.
expertTake: The Honda HSS928 is the best gas machine here for its commercial-grade engine and track drive, the AMERISUN 24-inch is the value pick, and the Poulan Pro 18-inch single-stage fits small paved drives. Skip gas altogether if your driveway is short and paved and you dislike fuel storage: a battery or corded machine will serve you with far less upkeep.
introParagraphs: Gas remains the benchmark for clearing big storms because an engine does not run down halfway through the driveway. It turns a gearbox that spins an auger and an impeller, and it keeps doing so in wet, heavy and plowed-in drifts that stall weaker motors. That sustained output is the reason these machines still dominate long driveways.

The tradeoff is ownership. A carbureted engine wants fresh fuel, seasonal oil, a plug now and then and a few minutes of attention before the first storm. This guide compares engine class, drive system, intake size and build so you can see where the money goes, and which machine suits compact paved drives versus long, sloped ones.

products.name: Honda HSS928 28-Inch Two-Stage Track Drive
products.description:
Honda builds the HSS928 around its commercial-grade GX270 overhead-valve engine, the same family of powerplant used on generators and construction equipment. That engine is the main reason owners pay more: it tends to start reliably, run smoothly and last for many seasons. The 28-inch path and throw of up to 52 feet make it a big-driveway tool.

The dual rubber tracks are the other differentiator. Compared with wheels, tracks keep more rubber on the ground, which helps on slopes, ice and the loose base of a gravel or packed driveway, and they reduce the tendency to wander when the auger loads. The downside is cost and weight, and tracks are slower to turn in a tight space.

Against the budget 24-inch models, it gives up value but wins on service life and resale. Plan on seasonal oil, a fresh plug when due and fuel stabilizer at season end. The electric start works from a wall outlet, which is welcome on bitter mornings. Parts and dealer support are broad, which matters in year five.
products.bestFor: Large, sloped or gravel-based driveways where traction and engine life matter.
pros: Commercial-grade GX270 engine built for long service
Dual rubber tracks hold grip on slopes and ice
28-inch path reduces passes on big driveways
Throws up to 52 feet for tall banks
cons: Highest price tier in this guide
Heavy and slow to turn in tight spaces

products.name: Ariens ST28DLE Deluxe 28-Inch Two-Stage
products.description:
Ariens is a dedicated snow-equipment maker, and the ST28DLE Deluxe is its 28-inch two-stage with electric start. A 28-inch width and a two-stage layout give it the same capacity class as the Honda, which makes it a serious option for a long driveway.

The difference from the Honda is drive: this is a wheeled machine, not a tracked one, so it is lighter on the ground and easier to turn but gives up some grip on ice-covered slopes. Compared with the budget PowerSmart models, the draw is the brand's dealer network, parts supply and design maturity.

Ownership follows the usual gas routine. Change the oil each season, replace the shear pins with the exact spec, and run stabilizer through the carburetor before spring storage. Because the listing carries little detail beyond the model name, confirm engine and chute specifics with the seller before buying.
products.bestFor: Owners who want a dedicated-brand 28-inch machine with dealer support.
pros: Dedicated snow-equipment maker with a long parts trail
28-inch two-stage clears long driveways quickly
Electric start avoids cold recoil pulls
Wheeled design turns more easily than tracks
cons: Wheels give up some grip to tracked rivals
Heavy and wants a flat storage floor
Listing is sparse, so verify specs

products.name: AMERISUN 24-Inch 212cc Self-Propelled Two-Stage
products.description:
AMERISUN offers a 7-horsepower, 212cc overhead-valve engine in a 24-inch two-stage with self-propelled drive and a claimed 45-foot throw, all at a low price tier. On paper it matches the mid-priced competition, which is exactly the point.

The tradeoff is refinement. Plastics, controls and documentation tend to be thinner than on the established brands, and parts and service rely on generic 212cc supplies rather than a dealer network. If you are comfortable doing basic small-engine upkeep, that is a fair swap.

Compared with the Honda, you give up track drive, engine pedigree and width, but you also keep a meaningful sum. Treat the machine as a seasonal tool: drain or stabilize fuel at season end, change the oil and keep spare shear pins and a spark plug on a shelf. A 24-inch path is plenty for a two-car driveway.
products.bestFor: Budget buyers who want a self-propelled two-stage for a typical suburban driveway.
pros: 7 HP 212cc engine in a self-propelled two-stage
Electric start included
24-inch path suits a two-car driveway
Low price tier among full two-stage machines
cons: No dealer network, so DIY service
Wheels only, with less grip than tracks

products.name: PowerSmart 24-Inch 212cc Two-Stage Self-Propelled
products.description:
This PowerSmart pairs a 212cc four-cycle engine with steel augers and a high-speed impeller, with a claimed 2,400 pounds per minute and a throw of up to 45 feet. The 20-inch intake height can take up to about 12 inches of snow in one pass, and 13-inch snow tires carry the weight.

It is nearly the same machine as the AMERISUN 24-inch on paper, so the choice comes down to price, availability and listing detail. PowerSmart's listing carries more spec data, which helps when you compare.

Expect the usual gas ownership: oil each season, stabilized fuel and a periodic plug. Steel augers and a steel impeller resist jamming in wet snow, though a stray stick or ice chunk will still shear a pin.
products.bestFor: Homeowners wanting well-documented 212cc power for a standard driveway.
pros: Steel augers and impeller resist wet-snow clogging
20-inch intake handles up to about 12 inches
13-inch snow tires add traction
Clear spec sheet for comparing
cons: Budget plastics on chute and controls

products.name: AMERISUN 26-Inch 212cc Two-Stage with LED Headlight
products.description:
The AMERISUN 26-inch stretches the same 212cc engine across a wider housing, with a 20-inch intake and a listing that claims driveways up to 12 parking spaces. A wider path means fewer passes, and the LED headlight helps for early clearing.

Because the engine is the same size as the 24-inch, the extra width loads it harder, so it may slow in dense, wet snow where the 252cc models keep going. It is a good match for long driveways with moderate snow.

As with all gas machines, keep fuel fresh, change oil and carry shear pins. The wider body is harder to store and turn.
products.bestFor: Long driveways with moderate snowfalls and a limited budget.
pros: 26-inch path cuts passes on long driveways
Six forward speeds suit varied snow
LED headlight for dark mornings
Low price for the width
cons: Wider body is awkward to store

products.name: Poulan Pro 18-Inch 99cc Single-Stage Gas
products.description:
Poulan Pro makes a gas single-stage: a 99cc four-stroke engine turns a steel-reinforced rubber auger that scrapes the pavement and throws snow in one step. The 18-inch path and a 190-degree remote chute are aimed at small to medium paved drives, walks and patios.

A single-stage gas machine is lighter and easier to maneuver than a two-stage, with no separate impeller or drive wheels to maintain. Compared with the Honda, it is a different class: it handles lighter snowfalls and cannot take on gravel or deep drifts.

Ownership is simple: fresh fuel, seasonal oil and a periodic look at the auger paddles. Because there is no separate drive system, you push it forward yourself.
products.bestFor: Small paved drives and walkways where a two-stage is overkill.
pros: Light and maneuverable for a gas machine
Steel-reinforced rubber auger is gentle on pavement
190-degree remote chute
Electric start included
cons: Not for gravel or deep drifts

buyingCriteria.explanation: A commercial-grade engine such as the Honda GX270 in the HSS928 is built for long duty cycles, while a generic 212cc in the AMERISUN or PowerSmart is built to a price. Displacement alone does not tell you durability. Pay for engine pedigree if you expect to keep the machine more than a decade. If you plow-clear the same drive for ten winters, spending more on the engine usually costs less than replacing a cheaper machine once.

Tracks, as on the Honda HSS928, keep more rubber on the ground and hold grip on slopes and ice. Wheels like the 13-inch snow tires on the PowerSmart are lighter and turn tighter. Pick tracks if your driveway slopes or has a loose base.

The Poulan Pro 18-inch is a single-stage that scrapes pavement, suited to light snow on paved drives. The two-stage machines add an impeller for deep snow, long throws and gravel. Pick by driveway surface and snow depth, not by price. A simple test is whether you ever clear gravel or a plowed windrow; if yes, only a two-stage with raised skid shoes is safe.
A 26-inch path on a 212cc engine, as on the AMERISUN 26-inch, loads the motor more than a 24-inch on the same engine. Wider is only an advantage if the engine can sustain it in wet snow.

Electric start spins the engine from a 120-volt outlet, which saves effort and helps in cold. All of the two-stage machines here offer it, and so does the Poulan Pro. A recoil backup is still worth having if the outlet is far away. Keep the cord and outlet in mind: a 120-volt start needs a grounded outdoor outlet within reach of the storage spot.
A dealer network, as with Ariens and Honda, shortens downtime. Generic 212cc machines rely on common parts you can order yourself. Decide which approach you will actually follow before buying.

specDecoder.meaning: Overhead valve engines place valves above the piston for better breathing and lower emissions. It is the standard layout for modern small engines.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Honda GX270, AMERISUN and PowerSmart all use OHV.

specDecoder.meaning: Small-engine horsepower figures are often gross numbers and vary by maker. Torque and gearing matter more in practice. Treat the number as a label, not a promise.
specDecoder.watchFor: AMERISUN quotes 7 HP for its 212cc; the Poulan Pro 99cc is much smaller.

specDecoder.meaning: The tallest pile the housing can take in one pass. It sets how deep a snowfall you can handle without layering.
Rubber tracks replace wheels for more contact patch and better slope traction. They add weight and slow turning.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the Honda HSS928 here uses tracks.

specDecoder.meaning: A maker's estimate of snow moved under ideal conditions. It compares poorly across brands.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Honda title cites up to 1,900 lb/min while PowerSmart cites 2,400.

howWeEvaluated.title: Engine and drivetrain
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared engine class, from the Honda GX270 to generic 212cc units and the 99cc Poulan Pro. We also weighed drive systems, tracks against wheels. Machines with proven engines scored higher on long-term value.

howWeEvaluated.title: Intake and path
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared path width from 18 to 28 inches and intake height up to 20 inches. We matched wider machines to engines that can sustain the load. A machine whose width exceeds what its engine can feed in wet snow was marked down.

howWeEvaluated.title: Maintenance and service access
howWeEvaluated.description: We scored how easy each machine is to keep running, including dealer support on the Honda and Ariens versus DIY parts on the AMERISUN and PowerSmart.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cold-weather behavior
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at electric start, throttle behavior and fuel system design, since cold starts are where cheap gas machines suffer. Owner feedback patterns shaped the scoring.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated the AMERISUN 24-inch as the value pick from the Honda as the premium pick, scoring the Poulan Pro for the small-drive niche.

cards.label: Tracks
cards.text: The Honda HSS928 keeps more rubber on the ground and holds grip on slopes and ice. It is heavier and slower to turn.

cards.label: Wheels
cards.text: The Ariens, AMERISUN and PowerSmart models are lighter and turn tighter but give up some traction on slick slopes.

howToChoose.note: Choose tracks for slopes and loose bases, wheels for flat drives and tight garages.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for steel augers, a steel impeller and enough engine torque to avoid bogging. Wet snow can weigh several times powder.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The PowerSmart 24-inch uses steel augers and an impeller that resist clogging, and the Honda's GX270 has the most torque reserve.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if your driveway is long, sloped or gravel-based, which points to the Honda HSS928 for its engine and tracks.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if the driveway is flat and paved. The AMERISUN 24-inch or Poulan Pro 18-inch does the job at a lower tier.

maintenance.why: Cold starts dilute oil with moisture and fuel. Fresh oil protects bearings under load.
Old fuel gums the carburetor jets. Run the engine dry or add stabilizer.
A fouled plug is the most common cold-start problem.
Shear pins protect the gearbox by breaking first. Carry correct spares.

maintenance.task: Inspect skid shoes and scraper bar
maintenance.why: These wear parts set the gap above the pavement. Replace when thin.

faq.q: Is a bigger engine always better?
faq.a: Not always. Torque, gearing and auger design decide real performance. A 212cc engine is plenty for most two-car driveways.

faq.q: Are tracks worth the extra cost?
faq.a: On slopes, ice or a loose gravel base, yes. On a flat paved driveway, wheels are fine and easier to turn.

faq.q: How long does a gas snow blower last?
faq.a: With oil changes and fresh fuel, a quality engine such as the Honda GX270 can last many seasons. Budget engines often last fewer.

faq.q: Can a single-stage gas machine replace a two-stage?
faq.a: For light snow on paved drives, yes. For deep snow or gravel, no.
Use fresh gasoline with stabilizer and avoid long-term ethanol blends in storage. Drain the carburetor before summer.
It saves effort and helps in cold. All the two-stage machines here include it.
